Confabulation in Dementia: Constantly Compensating Memory Systems

Ing-Mari Tallberg

Ing-Mari Tallberg

(Stockholm)

Ing-Mari Tallberg  

discourse, consciousness, common retrieval

The aim of the present paper is to examine the phenomenon of provoked confabulation at a discourse level and in relation to cognition and motivation. The basic assumption is that confabulation is an effect of a combination of poor memory functions and an altered level of awareness. It is also assumed that compensatory activation of memory processes takes place automatically. The speech of four women with dementia who exhibited episodes of confabulation was analyzed. The analysis focused on the relation between memory processes and movements between cognitive situations in the confabulate speech. It was found that perceptual and stable semantic knowledge seemed to activate automatically and compensate for poor episodic memory, specific semantic knowledge, and working memory. In these women with dementia, the automatic retrieval process compensated for poor access to knowledge and served to preserve the premorbid self-image. These findings have implications for the question of unconscious motivation possibly affecting the content of confabulations.

Commentary on “Confabulation in Dementia: Constantly Compensating Memory Systems”

John DeLuca

John DeLuca

(Newark, NJ)

John DeLuca  

Ing-Mari Tallberg has conducted a unique and complex linguistic analysis of confabulation in four patients, with the goal of discussing confabulation in light of theories of consciousness and memory.

Although selective in her choice of theories utilized, the author presents a logical and coherent study of how these constructs interact. While the selectivity in theories discussed makes this complex analysis easier to comprehend, it also constricts the potential gener-alizability of the findings to broader discussions of consciousness, memory, and confabulation. However, I find the intellectual arguments made thought-provoking and enticing.

John DeLuca: Professor of Physical Medicine & Rehabilitation, UM-DNJ-New Jersey Medical School; Director of Neuroscience Research and Vice President for Research Training, Kessler Medical Rehabilitation Research and Education Corporation, West Orange, NJ, U.S.A.

Douglas Watt

Douglas Watt

Douglas Watt  

In the exploding fields of affective and cognitive neuroscience, integrative treatments and heuristic reviews of literature become all the more critical for the overburdened clinician or researcher struggling to stay current as literature proliferates exponentially around nearly every single important topic. Psychoanalytic clinicians, hungry to digest the latest findings with respect to the neuroscience of emotion, find integrative reference materials particularly valuable. With respect to the critical domain of affective neuroscience, is there any version of a Bible in the field? Many might say that Jaak Panksepp's seminal textbook, Affective Neuroscience, published in 1998 comes as close as anything, and regular readers of this journal have presumably had a solid exposure to Dr. Panksepp's views and important contributions. The relatively recent Handbook of Affective Sciences, part of the ongoing Oxford University Press Series in Affective Science, is perhaps the most exhaustive (and exhausting?) treatment of emotion to date. Its coverage is encyclopedic, its breath of scholarship is generally quite impressive, and, unfortunately, its weight and size (and price!) are quite commensurate. Indeed, this textbook gives new meaning to the expression “it's not light reading,” weighing in at almost 8 pounds. If you plan on taking this in your briefcase to catch up a bit, let's hope your back is in good shape! Of course, this is not a real criticism, and one cannot expect such breadth of coverage in a lightweight highly portable volume. However, one does oftentimes end up wishing that one could purchase a PDF version of this reference work.

The volume is organized in terms of ten major topic headings: Basic/Core Neuroscience; Autonomic Psycho-physiology; Genetics and Development; the Expression of Emotion; Cognitive Components of Emotion; Personality; Emotion and Social Processes; Evolutionary and Cultural Perspectives on Affect; Emotion in Psychopathology; and

Emotion and Health. Leading authors and researchers contributed chapters. With respect to core neuroscience issues, there are chapters by the Antonio Damasio, Ralph Adolphs, and Hannah Damasio (“Contributions of the Lesion Method to the Functional Neuroanatomy of Emotion”) Kent Ber-ridge (“Comparing the Emotional Brains of Humans and Other Animals”), and Rebecca Elliott and Raymond Dolan (“Functional Neuroimaging of Depression: A Role for the Medial Prefrontal Cortex”). Under the section on Autonomic Psychophysiology, there are excellent review chapters by Gerhard Stemmler and by Wilfrid Janig. There is a competent summary of fear learning and fear conditioning in amygdaloid networks by Kevin LaBar and Joe LeDoux. The chapter by Kent Berridge, in the Core Neuroscience section, is a very strong contribution, perhaps the best, most integrative, and balanced statement about the neural substrates of emotion in the volume, although the chapter by the Damasios and Ralph Adolphs is also excellent. It is worth reading carefully front to back.

Research Digest

Peter Freed and Oliver Turnbull

Oliver Turnbull

(New York)

(Bangor, U.K.)

Oliver Turnbull  

Prejudice, Addiction, and Self-Awareness

Harris, L. T. & Fiske, S. T. (2006). Dehumanising the lowest of the low: Neuroimaging responses to extreme out-groups. Psychological Science, 17: 847-853.

Trying to understand the origins of cruelty to other human beings has always been difficult, perhaps because the examples are so diverse, ranging as they do from lone murderers to the cooperative actions of organized genocide. However, accounts of inhumanity tend to share a common theme: the victims are viewed as radically “different” and somehow less human. Indeed, atrocities on a scale that requires group coordination may be impossible unless the victims can be regarded as an out-group of one description or another. It also seems likely that all humans experience some of these feelings toward those we are prejudiced against, even though we tend not to act on these opinions. To investigate this phenomenon, Harris and Fiske devised functional-imaging studies of different social groups, using a sample of U.S. undergraduate students. Known empathy-related brain regions in medial prefrontal cortex (reviewed in previous editions of this Digest) were activated when viewing positively regarded empathy-inducing groups, such as those inducing pride (U.S. Olympic athletes), or pity (the elderly and disabled), or even envy (rich people). A key difference occurred when viewing less well regarded groups, which included drug addicts and the homeless. Remarkably, activation of this medial prefrontal cortex region was entirely absent when viewing these images. Instead, there was activation of a brain region (the insula) that is often associated with feelings of disgust. Naturally, the study might be interpreted as showing something rather negative about the nature of Princeton University students in the United States—namely, that they have a poorly developed social conscience. However, the central outcome is a clear set of brain findings related to an important social marker. The study clearly offers many possibilities for studying out-groups of many different sorts and also suggests the potentially far-reaching use of this tool in a “diagnostic” setting, most obviously in conditions (such as sociopathy and autistic-spectrum disorders) that are traditionally regarded as having low empathy.

International Society of Neuro-Psychoanalysis, Toronto Group

Iréne Matthis , Maggie Zellner and James Deutsch

James Deutsch

deutsch@utoronto.ca

James Deutsch  

Now into its sixth year, the Toronto Group continues to attract a diverse range of clinical and research people. The focus this year is on the integration of case material with theoretical efforts to formulate a more comprehensive and psychoanalytically based view of the mind, in contrast to the more reductionist—albeit burgeoning and fascinating—view from the neurosciences.

Both at a Toronto Group meeting in September 2006, as well as at the Freud 150th Anniversary meeting at the Canadian Psychoanalytic Society and Quebec English Branch in Montreal, Chair Dr. James Deutsch spoke of how the various points of view of psychoanalysis, stemming from Freud's own groundbreaking work with neurological patients, can contribute to diagnostic clarity, formulation, and treatment in neurological patients.

The focus was on a middle-aged patient who suffered an infarct of the right basal ganglia and anterior limb of the internal capsule, resulting in severe impairments in the domains of neu-ropsychological cognition, affect, and conation (will, initiation). Parkinson-like symptoms such as inability to initiate action or thought and severe restriction in range of affect, presumably partly based in the neuropathology, could be seen as additionally burdened by conflict related to feared consequences, in turn related to early trauma and pathological introjects operative within the superego.

From a structural point of view, “neurological symptoms” could be increasingly viewed as functioning partly defensively. It was possible to analyze the contribution of the harsh and punitive superego, manifesting in part as a sense of responsibility for outcomes that realistically belonged to others, and the patient's sense of his disability as a warranted punishment involving loss of key functions such as memory and decision-making, as well as a symbolic castration evidenced by indications of underlying fantasies regarding the actual brain anatomy involved in his injury. Emotional constriction was relieved with work on his early experiences of emotional expression and underlying drives as dangerous. Increasingly, the patient was able to sense himself as an active agent in his own recovery.

Commentary on “Toward a Neuroscience of Empathy: Integrating Affective and Cognitive Perspectives”

India Morrison

India Morrison

Gothenburg, Sweden.

India Morrison  

Predicates of Compassion

The affective feelings accompanying empathy are what make it what it is: an engine for positive social interactions, a relief from psychic solitude, and a fascinating object of study. Watt presents a framework in which attachment and prosocial motivation guide multiple aspects of affective and cognitive responses associated with empathy.

Here, both affective resonance and the motivation to improve the sufferers' affective state are core components of a “full emotional empathy.” He argues that without these components, any response or feeling on the part of the observer would fall short of empathy in this sense. In this perspective, attempts to operational-ize empathy in terms of other variables are considered to be of limited relevance in exploring its neural correlates. In particular, Watt criticizes research focusing on motor processing for failing to capture empathy's inherent affective element.

I am in wholehearted agreement that affect and motivation lie at the core of many phenomena that we would label as empathy (Morrison, 2007). However, in investigating the underlying neural systems, I believe that the motivational-affective elements involved in empathy can be fruitfully operationalized in terms of lower-level responses, motor-related responses in particular (Morrison, 2007; Morrison, Lloyd, di Pellegrino, & Roberts, 2004; Morrison, Peelen, & Downing, 2007; Morrison, Poliakoff, Gordon, & Downing, 2007). In what follows I would like to use my agreement with Watt's basic position on the importance of affect as a springboard to make the case for two points on which I differ from him.

The first is that although affective processing is not a property of the action-related premotor pathways in which mirror neurons are found, mirror-like mechanisms may nevertheless be a property of motivational-affective premotor pathways, removing the need to posit an intervening variable between motor and affective processing. The second is that the level at which these motivational-affective systems operate—specifically in mediating bodily safety— predicates fullblown compassionate responses, so that mechanisms on this level exist and can be studied independently of the drive to relieve others' distress in any given instance.

Commentary on “Toward a Neuroscience of Empathy: Integrating Affective and Cognitive Perspectives”

Larry Sandberg and Fredric Busch

Fredric Busch

Center for Psychoanalytic Training and Research, New York, NY, U.S.A.

Fredric Busch  

We are pleased to offer commentary on the scholarly and ambitious contribution of Douglas Watt to the neuroscience of empathy. In the brief space allotted, we will be selective in approaching the task, first addressing what we see as some of the central arguments of the paper and then turning to clinical psychoanalysis in an effort to encourage the kind of interdisciplinary dialogue for which this journal is designed. Implicit in this approach is the view that psychoanalytic perspectives on empathy are relevant to any comprehensive neuroscience of this complex phenomenon.

We shall critique Watt's perspectives on the use of animal data for a model of human neurophysiological and psychological functioning, the idea of contagion and its subcortical roots as “paradigmatic” for empathy, and the notion of gated resonance induction. Watt's conception of empathy will then be contrasted with a view that emphasizes the importance of mirror neuron systems and embodied simulation. We then turn to data from the psychoanalytic literature before suggesting a tentative, albeit partial, synthesis of the current neu-roscientific data in light of empirical psychoanalytic evidence. This synthesis acknowledges the omnipresent role of contagion while placing greater emphasis on the concepts of simulation, embodiment, and action as expressed through the closely related phenomena of enactment and transference/countertransference in the clinical situation.

Animal observation and empathy

Watt defines empathy as a “virtual synonym” of compassion, making suffering and its relief central features of his definition. We see this preference as motivated, in part, by an adoption of the “heuristic value to first developing an animal model … and then testing this against the more complex process in humans.” The “simple animal paradigm” used as an initial “template for the study of empathy in humans” is the response of maternal mammals to separation-distress signals. In other words, the focus on suffering is governed by the value placed not only on animal research, but particular animal research that looks at distressed infants and maternal responses. The literature is robust and convincing in elaborating the centrality of attachment/maternal behavior as a response to infant distress (Hofer, 2005). However, using animal models as a template for a complex function like empathy has potential pitfalls, including the lack of subjective data (Panksepp, 1998), differences between the neural systems of humans and other animals (Davidson, 2003), and the potential overemphasis on subcortical systems (Posner, Russell, & Peterson, 2005).

Rouw, R., & Scholte, H. S. (2007). Increased Structural Connectivity in Grapheme-Color Synesthesia.Nature Neuroscience, 10: 792-797.

Peter Freed

Peter Freed

1051 Riverside Drive, NY 10032, New York, U.S.A. (email: peterfreed@gmail.com)

Peter Freed  

Analysts typically instruct novice analysands—and frequently must remind professionals—to free-associate. By this it is meant that the patient should be encouraged to allow one idea, thought, feeling, or perception to lead to another and that this second link in the chain should be verbalized. By following the chain wherever it leads, it is hoped that the outlines of unconscious beliefs, fears, and fantasies may become visible and eventually allow the patient greater control over his/her mind, and ostensibly greater happiness. Of course, free association is something of a holy grail: aimed for, but rarely achieved. The conventional interpretation of failures of free association is that the patient—who, for example, demonstrates a dearth of connected ideas—is inhibiting or repressing or voluntarily filtering his/her associated ideas. Dynamic interpretations of failures of association are therefore possible.

In contrast, it is not at all conventional to suggest that patients may differ in their capacity for association as a function of wiring differences in their brains. Synesthesia—a phenomenologically defined neurological disorder in which sensory qualities from one domain are associated with sensations in another, or with thoughts or perceptions—may offer something of a challenge to this view. In synesthesia, a patient may automatically “see” a particular color with certain numbers. For example, Daniel Tammet, who can recite the first 22,500 decimal places of pi from memory, does so by simply seeing colors and shapes associated with each number unfold in his mind's eye, and he then simply calls out the number associated with each; what for others would be an impossible feat is for him as simple as watching a movie.

In their recent study, Rouw and Scholte shed light on the neural basis for this capacity. They used diffusion tensor imaging to visualize differences in the white matter of 18 subjects with word-color synesthesia versus 18 age-matched controls. Diffusion tensor imaging (DTI) is an MRI technique that takes advantage of the fact that while hydrogen ions (protons) can diffuse in any direction they like in grey matter (neuron cell bodies), in white matter their diffusion is distinctly limited. The myelin sheaths surrounding axons act, essentially, as river banks, funneling protons down their axons, which is referred to, logically enough, as anisotropy. By imaging the diffusion of protons over time, proton movement is used to visualize white matter tracts and, importantly, can be used to detect differences in connectivity in the brains of different populations of patients.

Diego Cohen , Beatriz Lerner , Marcelo Rodríguez , Valeria Guirland , Iréne Matthis and Maggie Zellner

Maggie Zellner  

Mentalization as the link between brain/mind in personality disorders.

This is a synthesis of the Chapter's discussions during the first six months of 2006, centered on an analysis of a keynote lecture given by Peter Fonagy (2005) at the 44th IPA Congress, “Attachment, Trauma and Psychoanalysis: Where Psychoanalysis Meets Neuroscience” and the paper by Gabbard (2005) “Mind, Brain, and Personality Disorders.”

In recent years there has been a growing interest in the idea of integrating and complementing the theories on the etiology of personality disorders by using findings from investigations of the nature-nurture interaction. Gabbard (1994, 2005) argues that the psychoanalytically oriented psychiatrist who is interested in the treatment of these disorders should begin to think as much in terms of psychodynamic forces, conflict, and defense mechanisms as in terms of genetic polymorphism, neuro-circuits, genome-environment interaction, pharmaco-dynamics, etc. Studies of ethology, epidemiology, and populations at risk for personality disorders arising from early adverse traumatic experiences have led us to posit the following from the point of view of the brain-mind relationship in borderline personality disorder (BPD) and antisocial personality disorder (ASPD) disorders (Caspi et al., 2002; Schore, 1994):

The development of the brain/mind requires input from the environment. Although the brain is not a clean slate even at birth, since intrauterine environment facilitates brain/mind development, it appears that after birth affective relationships exert a powerful influence on neuronal growth and synaptic connection, which underlie the shaping of neuro-anatomical structures, which then mediate the affective regulation process including internalization and memory of positive interactions with the primary object (Bateman & Fonagy, 2003; Gabbard, 1994; Schore, 1994). According to Bowlby (1969, 1988), the brain/mind stores patterns of emotional interaction with objects that constitute internal working models, or, in more contemporary terms, primitive self-representations in interaction with an object that are joined by a range of affects (Fonagy, Gergely, Jurist, & Target, 2002).

[[RunningHead]]

Commentary on “Confabulation in Dementia: Constantly Compensating Memory Systems”

Simone Hoermann

Simone Hoermann

(New York)

Simone Hoermann  

Ing-Mari Tallberg investigates instances of confabula-tory speech in individuals with dementia from a linguistic viewpoint, and she draws parallels to cognitive models of memory and consciousness, as well as to the psychoanalytic concept of primary process. In doing so, the author builds on Solms's (2000) idea that in cases with brain dysfunction, implicit processes of the mind are revealed and that investigating the phenomenon of confabulation can provide insights into primary-process mental functioning. Tallberg states, quoting Solms (2000) and Turnbull, Jenkins, and Rowley (2004), that confabulations have qualities found in the special characteristics of the unconscious: tolerance of mutual contradiction, timelessness, replacement of external reality with psychic reality, and expression of an unconstrained activation of ideas.

The term “confabulation” has been used somewhat inconsistently in the literature, though it generally describes phenomena having to do with telling or acting upon false narratives or memories without intending to lie, and without awareness of these falsehoods (Gilboa et al., 2006). Confabulation has been observed and investigated in a number of different conditions, including dementia, Korsakoff syndrome, traumatic brain injury, or anterior communicating artery aneurysms (Hirstein, 2006).

In the present paper, Tallberg offers a linguistic definition of confabulation, stating that in confabulatory speech, the linguistic markers that serve to connect speech content to time, place, and person are used inadequately. The author links this definition to Tulving's (1985) concept of autonoetic consciousness, which allows individuals to be aware of their internal experiences over time, thus facilitating processes of episodic memory. In contrast, noetic consciousness allows individuals to think about something they know, and it is related to semantic memory. In addition, anoetic consciousness simply registers perceptions bound to the current situation. One might hypothesize that ano-etic consciousness may be related to implicit memory. Implicit memory has theoretically been linked to unconscious processes (Kandel, 1999).

Editors' Introduction

Oliver Turnbull and Yoram Yovell

Yoram Yovell

Yoram Yovell  

This issue's Target Article, by Ing-Mari Tallberg, is on linguistic aspects of confabulation, in patients with dementia. As usual, the article is followed by a set of commentaries by neuroscientists and psychoanalysts, who discuss various aspects of the article and also comment on larger theoretical questions.

In the Original Articles section, we publish four new articles: one by Norman Holland on laughter across species; one by Kobi Tiberg on the use of the Thematic Apperception Test in patients with right-hemisphere lesions; one by Mona Tondowski and colleagues on emotional experience in anosognosia; and, finally, one by Calvin Kai-Ching Yu on loss of dreaming after frontal-lobe lesions.

Also, we introduce a new section, entitled Clinical Reports. Our intention is to use this space for material that has a more clinical flavor, including brief accounts of work with patients using a more descriptive style. Our first article in this new section is by Mark Blechner and is a report of a small series of patients with panic disorder, considered in the light of existing accounts of the neurobiology of the phenomenon. We hope that this new section will diversify the sort of empirical material that we publish, and we would like to encourage submissions to this new facet of the journal.

As always, the issue ends with the Book Review, Research Digest, and International Bulletin sections. In this issue we offer a warm welcome to the new arrivals on our team: Peter Freed (in the Research Digest) and Maggie Zellner (in the International Bulletin).

Response to Commentaries on “Confabulation in Dementia: Constantly Compensating Memory Systems”

Ing-Mari Tallberg

Ing-Mari Tallberg

(Stockholm)

Ing-Mari Tallberg  

In “Confabulation in Dementia,” the approach was a combination of theories of discourse, cognition, and consciousness. The phenomenon of confabulation was explained as a dysdeictic retrieval process, which compensates for poor access to episodic memory and serves to preserve a premorbid self-image. The content of confabulations possibly is affected by unconscious motivation. Most controversial in the paper, I suspect, was the idea that confabulate utterances consist of preserved fragments of semantic knowledge retrieved in a cognitive system that is unconstrained due to poor executive functioning.

I am grateful for the interesting and sometimes critical responses and, having considered all initiated comments, will now try to bring my ideas a bit further. The commentaries on the paper strengthen my opinion that the use of a broad interdisciplinary approach is fruitful when it comes to such a complex phenomenon as confabulation. I think it is necessary to call attention to the scientific disciplines devoted to language and interaction, mainly linguistics, semantics, and sociolinguistics. After all, confabulation usually occurs as utterances that are aberrant and are created in interaction. Linguistics concerns the study of how human languages are structured, acquired, and used, and the linguistic sciences provide tools for analysis of language production and interaction. Semantics, and especially the semantic-pragmatic section, concerns meaning and how meaning is created in context, a very relevant topic in confabulation (see, e.g., Caplan, 1992; Lakoff, 1987; Levinson, 1983). One major advantage with the linguistic methods is that they enable analysis of utterances as products and that this can be done without considering the cognitive level of subjects. Linguistic studies of interaction in dementia and aphasia have contributed to the knowledge of irrelevant speech (see, e.g., Anward, 2003; Hamilton, 1994; Shakespeare, 1998).

Mark Blechner provided comments from a psychoanalytic perspective. In his response, confabulation and normality were discussed—an issue that I would like to comment on further. In addition, Blechner contributed with a description of confabulation in psychoanalytic patients and with observations on confabulation and interaction. Although I usually work within the neurolinguistic/neuropsychological field as a speech and language therapist, I recognize Blechner's point of view concerning interpersonal and affective factors as being very close to mine.

This Issue

Oliver Turnbull and David Olds

David Olds

David Olds  

This issue's Target Article and the associated Commentaries come to grips with a central issue in the theory of empathy, and indeed of affective neuroscience. This is the question of how affects are subjectively experienced and communicated. At issue is the level at which empathy can occur. Does it begin with cortical appreciation via the mirror neuron system and then produce an “embodied simulation” of the affect, or is empathy the gated “contagion” of emotion which immediately engages the deepest neurological brainstem centers? The debate hinges on the emphasis placed on the mirror neuron system, as opposed to a direct contagion by an as-yet-unknown mechanism. Thus the author and the extremely articulate commentators are grappling with one of the most crucial issues in affect theory today.

Here we offer a few introductory remarks with an eye to integrating the Target Article and Commentaries. The paper, in the tradition of Dr. Watt's other writings, is an encyclopedic review of what is known about empathy, all the way up to the cutting edge. One crucial part of his model is that empathy is a gated resonance system by which one person apprehends the emotional state of another. Gating refers to the fact that certain “gates” open one to greater empathy: attachment and affectionate bonds with the other, the inherent em-pathic capacities of the empathizing person, the youth and “cuteness” of the other, a positive emotional state toward the other. These factors are not particularly controversial. The major controversy arises from an issue that goes back a long way in academic psychology—namely, the respective roles of cognition and emotion. Until very recently academic psychology focused on the cognitive aspects of the brain and tended to ignore the emotion systems. Jaak Panksepp is one of the leaders of the revolution that brought emotion into center stage and that, in fact, brought in the emotions of other animals. And this was against much resistance.

A Farewell from Yoram Yovell

Yoram Yovell MD PHD

Yoram Yovell

Israel

Yoram Yovell  

I have been privileged to serve on the Editorial Board of Neuro-Psychoanalysis for the last five years. All good things come to an end, however, and saying goodbye, although necessary due to new obligations and commitments, is not easy. I believe the readers of this journal will have no difficulty empathizing with the excitement and the deep satisfaction I experienced while editing a publication that documented the emergence of a new interdisciplinary field, as well as a scientific paradigm shift in the making. As our field has come of age, so has our journal, and I feel fortunate to have been there when it happened. But in addition to the intellectual rewards of editing a journal that brings together some of the finest and most creative minds in psychoanalysis and the cognitive neurosciences, I was blessed with the opportunity to meet and work with an extraordinary group of people.

During these five years Dr. Oliver Turnbull, my Co-Editor, has become a close personal friend as well as the object of my quiet admiration. He continues to shoulder most of the day-to-day burden of running the journal with grace, talent, and tact. The ability to make and communicate difficult editorial decisions, and to ensure that the journal is typeset, printed, and distributed on time, requires endless patience and perseverance. Fortunately for all of us, Oliver has both. Patricia Porter, our administrator, quickly became an indispensable member of our editorial team. In fact, I suspect that without her, the readers of this journal might have had a lot less to read. The section editors, members of the Editorial Policy Committee, and members of the Editorial Advisory Board were all generous in contributing their time—arguably their most precious and perishable resource—to help make this journal become what it is today. I am greatly indebted to all of them. Dr. Mark Solms and Dr. Edward Ner-sessian, the founders and first Editors of this journal, continue to serve as a source of inspiration for all of us. But my greatest thanks go to the many colleagues who contributed their scientific work to our journal. The way they put up with our impossible deadlines and tolerated our not-always-gentle editorial touches never ceased to impress me. In the final analysis, it was their fine papers and commentaries that earned our journal the reputation it deserves.

Iréne Matthis , Maggie Zellner , Diego Cohen , Luz Mangino-Cohen , Beatriz Lerner and Marcelo Rodriguez

Marcelo Rodriguez

diegocohen@fibertel.com.ar

Luzclar1@hotmail.com

Marcelo Rodriguez  

Is neuroscientific knowledge useful to psychoanalysis?

The Psychoanalysis and Neuroscience Chapter of the Argentine Psychoanalytical Association, over which I preside, is in its fourth year of regular monthly meetings. On this occasion we have begun work on two recent papers—Pulver (2003) and Blass and Carmeli (2007)—about the usefulness of neuro-scientific knowledge to psychoanalysis. Pulver's observations triggered a series of reflections. Our first disagreement with the author is that, in fact, some neuroscientific knowledge has brought about changes in psychoanalytic techniques. The most relevant example is perhaps the introduction of psychopharma-cological treatment, which has led to the consideration of variations in the transference and countertransference, modification of the dream process, and other variables, such as the effects on the mind of the patient when the treatment is divided between a pharmacologist and a psychoanalyst.

We also wonder why a systematized domain of knowledge in permanent evolution—the field of psychoanalysis as well as neuroscience—must have a rapid application and purpose. Darwin's theory of evolution was better understood and appreciated decades later through Watson & Crick's double-helix structure of DNA, even though from the viewpoint of genetic laws, the idea of a certain life-transmittal substance had already been conceived. In our reading of the articles mentioned above, they struck us as having a defensive attitude that tended to isolate psychoanalysis from related disciplines, leading to a situation that Freud himself had not encouraged (Solms & Saling, 1986).

Pulver states that “it is hard to imagine a way in which analytic technique will be influenced by what the analyst knows about the functioning of the brain.” We might argue that this proposal ignores two facts; in the first place, theoretical epis-temology—since his position would lead to an acceptance of a dualistic division of the mind/brain, already outdated (Damasio, 1998). In simplistic terms, we would say that Pulver seems to presume that an analyst is concerned with the treatment of the mind, whereas a psychiatrist/neurologist/neurosurgeon, etc. is concerned with the brain, thus giving rise to a new split. Second, from the clinical viewpoint, we wonder if the analyst these days would not admit that some patients—for example with bipolar illness diagnosis (especially when found to be suffering from an acute manic episode) or schizophrenia—cannot be treated analytically without conceiving of modern theories of brain function.

In Memoriam

The Editors would like to record with sadness the passing of Clifford Yorke on June 20th in Oxfordshire, of Morton Reiser in New York on June 21st, and of Marjorie Pfeffer in New York on November 9th.

Clifford Yorke was a close colleague of Anna Freud. In his later career he had a growing enthusiasm about the emergence of neuropsychoanalysis, and some of his final publications are in this field. He was a member of the Editorial Advisory Board of our journal, and he contributed to its first two issues.

Morton Reiser was one of the early pioneers in bringing neuroscience to psychoanalysis. He had continued to be active in the field and co-authored an article published in the 2004:2 issue of our journal (Freud's Theory of Mind and Functional Imaging Experiments). He was also a member of our Editorial Advisory Board.

Marjorie Pfeffer maintained a long-standing association and commitment to our field. She was President of the Neuropsychoanalysis Foundation that funded the Arnold Pfeffer Center at the New York Psychoanalytic Institute, and she had tirelessly supported our field in innumerable ways.

All three of these long-standing supporters of neuropsychoanalysis will be missed.

Temporal Consciousness and Confabulation

How are different memory systems involved in confabulation? What is the role of consciousness in patients who confabulate? What determines the content of confabulation? Tallberg concentrates on these questions and proposes that, in confabulating patients, semantic memory activates automatically to compensate for poor episodic memory and working memory, that a higher level of awareness—namely autonoetic consciousness—is not reached, and that unconscious motivation toward the preservation of a positive self-image determines the positive emotional bias observed in the content of confabulation. We shall focus only on the first two questions and their responses. We do not consider in our commentary Tallberg's answer to the third question, because it is based on the assumption that intentionality can be attributed to a mechanism or a process that is not conscious and, by definition, is inaccessible to consciousness. This assumption itself would need a long commentary (for a discussion of this point, see Dalla Barba, 2002).

Does semantic memory compensate for poor episodic memory and poor working memory, as Tallberg suggests? Both the analysis of the reports provided by Tallberg's patients and what is known from the literature on confabulation support a positive answer to this question. Karin (Case 2, Example 3), when she was interviewed in her hospital room, reported that she was on a train, on a journey to Gothenburg. Editorial Transition

Oliver Turnbull

Oliver Turnbull

Bangor, U.K.

Oliver Turnbull  

This issue marks a transition in the editorial history of this journal, as Yoram Yovell stands down from his Editorial position. Yoram has been an Associate Editor since the 2002 issue and then Co-Editor since 2005. He has played a central role in the journal during this time, not only in dealing with the huge amount of work associated with organizing the Target Articles in each issue, but more generally in shaping editorial policy. In addition, he has often stepped in to deal with situations that were both “politically” and/or interpersonally difficult: situations that (I am acutely aware) arise all too often for those with editorial responsibilities. I am (and we should all be) deeply grateful to Yoram for his work with the journal during this time, and we are delighted that he will still remain associated with the journal, as he joins our Editorial Policy Committee.

Yoram's Editorial position will be taken by David Olds. David has been associated with the journal from its beginnings and was on the Editorial Board when the journal was founded in 1999. As many of our readers will know, David is a Psychiatrist at Columbia University in New York and a Training Psychoanalyst at the Colombia Psychoanalytic Center and the Berkshire Psychoanalytic Institute. He has had a long-term interest in integrating psychoanalysis with other disciplines and has written a number of important papers relating psychoanalysis to semiotics, neuroscience, and evolutionary psychology. David will have primary responsibility for the Target Articles in each issue. He is eminently qualified for this editorial work, though he is probably unaware of the magnitude of the task he has signed up for! On behalf of the entire journal team, we wish him all the best in his new role.

While public fascination with suppressed memories gravitates to the dramatic and scandalous variety, as in recovered memories of abuse (e.g., the American child-abuse cases of the 1990s) or suppressed knowledge of guilt (e.g., O. J. Simpson's claim that he did not kill his wife), analysts have long been intrigued by the more subtle types found in everyday life. How does a patient who fought with her husband before leaving for work function happily in a board meeting an hour later? And what brings her anger flooding back as she re-enters her house that evening? Furthermore, in line with the Rouw & Schulte study described above, what brain regions are likely activated—or deactivated—when patients recall long-suppressed memories during sessions?

The recent study by Depue, Curran, and Banich explores this question with an innovative fMRI design.

Tsetsenis, T., Xiao-Hong, M., lacono, L. L., Beck, S. G., & Gross, C. (2007). Suppression of conditioning to ambiguous cues by pharmacogenetic inhibition of the dentate gyrus.Nature Neuroscience, 10 (7): 896-902.

In psychoanalytic theory, signal anxiety heralds the imminent emergence into consciousness of an unacceptable thought. In terms of therapeutic technique, psychoanalysis has long distinguished itself from cognitive behavioral therapy in emphasizing the importance of uncovering these thoughts, working with them, and rendering them tolerable, rather than on enhancing the patient's suppressive capacity. In this sense, the anxiety is taken as a useful, but in itself unproblematic, marker of fearful thoughts that must be processed.

The possibility that patients differ genetically in their tendency to label internal stimuli as anxiety provoking throws some doubt on this formulation. In short, what if the problem with signal anxiety is not the underlying thought, or the signal itself, but, rather, the association between the two? This would carve out a middle ground between pharmacological strategies that simply seek to dampen anxiety symptoms and analytic ones that seek to explore anxious ideation. The neu-roanatomical analog of this hypothesis is the following: In analytic theory, amygdala activation signals the association of a stimulus with danger (which precedes, but is distinct from, the mobilization of autonomic arousal or instrumental responses). The amygdala activation per se is not considered problematic; what is problematic is the association of the stimulus with danger, occurring in memory-association regions such as the hippocampus.

In analytic theory, exploring this association may allow decoupling of the stimulus from the danger association through improved information processing in memory formation and retrieval regions. For example, a stimulus that only deserves moderate concern may be falsely tagged with high-danger status; the association mechanism may need to be fine-tuned to allow association with only moderate danger. In a wonderful recent study, Tsetsenis and colleagues exploited the known role of serotonergic (5HT) function in anxiety-dampening. They bred 5HT-1A knockout mice that had markedly decreased 5HT-1A receptor density in two brain regions, the amygdala and dentate gyrus, thereby anatomically releasing these regions from serotonergic control originating in the dorsal raphe nuclei. In an experimental paradigm, they taught mice to associate one tone with 100% predictable foot shock, and a second tone with only 60% predictable food shock. They then compared the anxiety (freezing) response to the two tones, in the absence of shock, in normal versus knockout mice. In this Pavlovian paradigm they found that while both mice demonstrated equal levels of anxiety to the 100% predictive tone, the knockout mice demonstrated the same level of anxiety to the 60% predictive tone. In contrast, the normal mice demonstrated an appropriately reduced level of anxiety to the 60% tone, thereby bestowing upon them a significant adaptive advantage. When the researchers reintroduced 5HT-1A receptors (the pharmacogenetic accomplishment of the study) into the amygdala, they globally reduced the mice's fear response to both tones.

“An Introduction to a Neuropsychoanalytic Perspective on Personality Disorders” was a one-day workshop initially presented in November 2006 at the annual congress of the Ordre des Psychologues du Quebec, the Quebec licensing board for psychologists. As the workshop was fully booked (attended by 90 clinical psychologists and neuropsychologists), we decided to repeat it after the congress, and a further 100 participants attended this time, including many psychiatrists. The same workshop was also held in Paris in November 2006 and drew a full room of 50 participants.

We have set up an ongoing seminar that is limited to 15 participants. It consists of one-day gatherings around specific themes. The first was held in January 2007. As this was the initial meeting, half of the day was devoted to functional neuro-anatomy. The second part of the day looked at epistemological issues in neuropsychoanalysis. The second seminar investigated affect, in terms of both neurodevelopment and the therapeutic setting. The third focused on memory, and the fourth on the neurodynamics of psychotherapy.

Our group is currently translating Allan Schore's Affective Regulation and the Disorders of the Self (2003). It will be published in French by our training institute's publishing section, the CIG Press. It should be available to French-speaking readers in the course of 2008.

Toronto Group, International Neuropsychoanalytic Society

Iréne Matthis , Maggie Zellner and James Deutsch

James Deutsch

j.deutsch@utoronto.ca

James Deutsch  

The Toronto Group, made up of diverse clinicians and researchers, has been grappling with the differences and overlaps between neuroscience and psychoanalysis, in particular the multiple perspectives that psychoanalysis brings to studying brain function in greater detail and complexity (e.g., conflict and defense) than hitherto with mainstream neuroscience methods.

Dr. Norman Doidge spoke, two months prior to its publication, about his new book, The Brain That Changes Itself (Doidge, 2007). He began with an enlightening discussion of the historic barriers (philosophical, political, religious, narcissistic) to the now accepted view of nervous tissue as malleable to experience throughout the lifespan. He pointed out how Freud, in the modern era, had anticipated by 60 years the concept of the learning synapse, of the principle of “use it or lose it.” If the brain is indeed a machine, it is one that is plastic, not fixed. Our human genetic heritage bestows the ability to learn new ways of learning. Unfortunately, in what the author terms the “plasticity paradox,” ruts or tracks can be formed, from repeated travels over the same plastic territory, limiting choice and possibility.

Doidge pointed out numerous examples of cortical reorganization, notably the efforts of researcher Michael Merzenich, in which, with a combination of support from others and the individual's motivated learning (which activates the nucleus basalis of Meynert and other nodes in reward circuits), remarkable changes can occur, in various neurological disease states. Processes previously assumed to be irrevocably tied to the peripheral components of movement and perception can be shifted using thought and perception alone.

Turning to issues commonly seen by psychoanalysts and other therapists, he pointed out the usefulness of the concept of the plasticity paradox in understanding idiosyncratic sexual tastes and addictions. Neurotic patients may be understood as having particular difficulty unlearning. As expected, numerous examples can be gleaned, from Freud's work onward, to illustrate technical difficulties encountered in trying to effect changes in character. It was in trying to understand what is involved in personality and its development that the discussion became most stimulating, as it is likely that not all brain areas are equally plastic, not all subjects are equally willing, and not all defenses are easily breached.

Bulletin 17: Introduction

Iréne Matthis and Maggie Zellner

Maggie Zellner

irene.matthis@swipnet.se

magsterz@gmail.com

Maggie Zellner  

We are happy this time to introduce two fully new member groups and one old/new group. For some time we have been hoping for a group in Asia, and now the wish has come true. Kazuyuki Hirao from Kyoto has been able both to start the first Japanese Neuro-Psychoanalytic Study Group and to publish the first translation in Japanese of Solms and Turnbull's The Brain and the Inner World. That is indeed a wonderful accomplishment, for which we congratulate him. At the same time Gilles Delisle, in Montreal, Canada, has initiated a new neuropsychoanalytic group, and this already has several projects running. It is also in the friendly city of Montreal that our next Congress will take place. Meanwhile, in Paris, Jean Benjamin Stora has rejuvenated the French group that for some time we had lost contact with. We welcome them back.

At the time of writing, the Congress in Vienna has just finished. Even if the subject was “depression”, most delegates seemed very happy about the presentations on the theme, the discussions, and the organization. As always we have to thank especially Paula Barkay, Pat Porter, and their team, working together with Gyuri Fodor in Vienna.

Please do not hesitate to contact me or Maggie Zellner if you have any questions or require information on our joint work.

The Japanese Neuro-Psychoanalytic Study Group in Kyoto

Iréne Matthis , Maggie Zellner and Kazuyuki Hirao

Kazuyuki Hirao

email: kazhirao@kuhp.kyoto-u.ac.jp

Kazuyuki Hirao  

The Japanese translation of The Brain and the Inner World, an introductory text to neuropsychoanalysis by Mark Solms and Oliver Turnbull, was published in July 2007. Our group, the Japanese Neuro-Psychoanalytic Study Group in Kyoto, was established on this occasion. This monumental book has now been published in seven languages. Currently there is a great distance between psychological (subjective) and biological (objective) perspectives in Japan, as there is elsewhere, which can be seen, for example, in the discrepancy between trends in biological psychiatry strongly promoting pharmacotherapy and traditional schools of psychotherapy. Quite a few people involved in the field of psychiatry and psychotherapy have voiced concerns about this state of affairs. We hope that this book and the field of neuropsychoanalysis itself will be able to help the Japanese people who are interested in bridging the gulf between those perspectives.

The activities of our group are as follows:

Clinical work. We are currently studying Clinical Studies in Neuro-Psychoanalysis by Mark Solms and Karen Kaplan-Solms and discussing clinical methods integrating neuroscience and psychoanalysis/psychotherapy, from both objective and subjective perspectives. Since most of us are psychiatrists/physicians and psychotherapists, we try to practice what we learn in our daily clinical work from this dual perspective.

Research. Most of us are engaged in studies of patients with psychiatric disorders from the viewpoint of affective and social neuroscience. We have recently investigated the relationships between brain and social cognition, such as mentalizing or empathy, using MRI. These mental functions are intimately associated with interpersonal relationships in psychotherapy—for example, transference. Thus we believe that these studies will help us to understand how psychotherapy works. We also plan a clinical study designed for the combination of pharmacotherapy (modulation of serotonin or dopamine) and psychotherapy (subjective experience) with neuroimaging methods (objective brain function).

Dr. Y. Soussumi is the General Coordinator and is responsible for the theoretical foundations and strategies in the implantation of the “Virada Social” Project of Social Development sponsored by Inst. Rukha, treating children and adolescents at social risk, as well as families and communities where they belong. This intervention is made by means of direct socioedu-cative actions, working in partnership with other institutions located in needy communities, aiming at the formation of a wider-reaching net allowing joint action. The Virada Project, based on neuropsychoanalytic principles developed from CEINP's studies and research, is focused on awareness and biopsychosocial and transcendental development of communities with minimal resources, as well as socially and economic privileged ones.

Dr. Soussumi is a Coordinator, together with Professor Dr. J. J. Mari, Professor Dr. M. Feijö, and Dr. A. R. L. Lima, of the partnership between Rukha/CEINP with UNIFESP (Federal University of Säo Paulo) for the development of studies and projects in the areas of neuropsychoanalysis, psychiatry, psychoanalysis, and the neurosciences. This partnership will work in mutual cooperation in the field of preventative and curative mental health in the Virada Project. The planned action will help in the study of the roots of violence and of situations that favor biopsychic pathologies such as PTSD and depression. Dr. Soussumi is a neuropsychoanalytic supervisor in the research “Early Stress and Mental Disease—A Study of the Impact of Early Maternal Separation in Children's Development and System of Reaction to Stress,” at the Psychiatric Department of UNIFESP, in conjunction with the Maternity Hospital Vila Nova Cachoei-rinha, with financial support from FAPESP (Foundation for Research Support in the State of S. Paulo).

Dr. Soussumi participated in the psychosomatics forum, promoted by the Brazilian Association of Psychosomatics, in the panel “Psychoneuroendocrinology and Neuro-Psychoanaly-sis,” in May 2007 in Säo Paulo; in the XXI Brazilian Congress of Psychoanalysis, as a member of the round table “Psychoanalysis in Face of Medical Advances,” in Porto Alegre; and in the Scientific Event from the Scientific Board as a Lecturer on “Reminding, Repeating, Working-Through: A Neuro-psycho-analytical Approach,” in May 2007.

Dream Recall and the Dissociation between Dream Cessation and Neurological Memory Disorders

Calvin Yu

Calvin Yu

10 Wai Tsui Crescent, Braemar Hill Road, North Point, Hong Kong (email: calyu2000@hotmail.com).

Calvin Yu  

axial amnesia, dream awareness, dream cessation, dream recall, frontal amnesia, neurological memory disorders

The human lesion method for the study of dreaming has been criticized on the grounds that patients' reports of dream cessation can be conceived as a secondary effect of memory failure, rather than as a direct consequence of neurological insults. There are two arguments within this criticism. First, dream recall is difficult in nature, even in normal people. Second, neurological patients' memories, and therefore their dream recall, are poor. This paper aims to determine whether dream recall is difficult in nature by summarizing the findings generated by the major methods utilized by researchers to study dream recall. Moreover, the controversy of dream cessation as a secondary effect of memory failure is examined, taking into consideration the clinical attributes of the major categories of neurological memory dysfunction. The analyses indicate an essential differentiation between memory failure and dream cessation.

Douglas Watt

Douglas Watt

email: dfwatt@rcn.com

Douglas Watt  

There is much to recommend in this erudite and very readable treatment by Gerald Edelman, presenting his thinking on the neural nature of consciousness and its implications for the integration of human knowledge and science. The title of the book reflects the massive scientific challenge of linking a picture of our own internal conscious nature to the larger Nature around us, with our internal nature reflecting, therefore, “a second nature.” The volume presents simple and easily digestible versions of important core concepts in Edelman's thinking about consciousness and the brain from many other publications and books, including neural Darwinism (natural ontogenetic selection of certain neurons and circuits over others during neural development, analogous to population selection in evolution), reentry (reciprocal connectivity of many widespread brain areas), degeneracy (that there are many circuits or neural systems potentially creating or contributing to the same behavior or function), and so forth. His discussions at the beginning of the book on the separation of the sciences and humanities, and on the separation even within the sciences between the sciences of complexity (such as psychology and neuroscience) versus the “hard sciences,” are elegantly argued and very much worth reading. He gives a very easily digested view of basic neuroanatomy and neural circuits and then launches into discussion of his core suppositions in terms of what neural processes in the brain support the creation of conscious states. Of course, such an understanding—a validated neuroscience of consciousness—would forge profound links between parts of the universe previously totally separated and would serve to heal ontological separations most famously (or infamously?) articulated by Descartes when he proposed that mind and matter were fundamentally separate things in the universe. In many ways Edelman's thinking about the brain and consciousness is a conceptual extension of his seminal and Nobel prize-winning work on immunology, where he realized that population selection mechanisms, analogous to evolutionary selection, were at the core of the immune system's success in responding to foreign proteins. In other words, his Nobel prize-winning insight was that the immune system did not work on some version of “information transfer” based on encounters with different foreign proteins but, rather, from selection processes operating on internal endogenous variations. This basic image of the brain as a selectionist system informs much of his thinking.

Cessation of Dreaming and Ventromesial Frontal-region Infarcts

Calvin Kai-Ching Yu

Calvin Kai-Ching Yu

(Hong Kong)

Calvin Kai-Ching Yu  

Freud attributed the primary instigator of dreaming to the “libidinal drive” in his theory. Research support for this classical psychoanalytic theory was provided in Solms's clinico-anatomical studies. He found that damage to the ventromesial frontal pathway caused both global cessation of dreaming and a reduction in motivated behaviour. However, most of the patients in Solms's clinical series were cases of tumor and diffuse injury. These conditions rendered the localization work difficult and imprecise. In view of this, the present study investigated the association between dream cessation and lesions to the ventromesial frontal region in patients who were diagnosed with infarctions. Solms's findings were largely replicated. In addition, results from the present study indicated that compared to the other neural components in the ventromesial frontal pathway, the role of the caudate nucleus appeared to be particularly salient in the functional architecture of dreaming.

Keywords: caudate nucleus, dream cessation, libidinal drive, motivational mesolombic dopaminergic pathway, nucleus accumbens, ventromesial frontal-region infarcts

Cessation of dreaming has long been observed in patients with frontal-lobe lesions (Corda, 1985; Epstein & Simmons, 1983; Gloning & Sternbach, 1953; Piehler, 1950). By using the clinico-anatomical method, Solms (1997) further suggested that global cessation of dreaming was associated with lesions in the white matter immediately surrounding the frontal horns of the lateral ventricles. The white matter of the frontal lobes of the brain just above the eyes contains a large fiber-pathway, which transmits dopamine from the ventral tegmentum to the higher parts of the brain. From this finding, Solms (1995, 1997, 1999, 2000) underscored that the primary function of this brain pathway, which is crucial for the generation of dreams, is to instigate goal-seeking behaviors and an organism's appetitive interactions with the world. In other words, the function of this important brain pathway is to motivate the subject to seek out and engage with external objects that, in turn, can satisfy his inner biological needs. These are precisely the functions that Freud (1900) attributed to the “libidinal drive”—the primary instigator of dreams in his theory. Accordingly, damage to this pathway causes cessation of dreaming, along with a dramatic reduction in motivated behaviour (Solms, 1997).

(Ap)perceptual Distortions in a Case of Right-Hemisphere Lesion: Evidence from the TAT

Kobi Tiberg

Kobi Tiberg

Raanana, Israel)

Kobi Tiberg  

anosognosia, perception, projection, RHD, narcissism, TAT

A diverse body of recent evidence suggests that patients with anosognosia to hemiplegia following right-hemisphere deficit (RHD) have implicit knowledge of their deficit and that their denial is motivated by the aversive emotional consequences that would accompany full awareness. Recent theories link spatial deficits following RHD with this defensive, psychological need, suggesting that atten-tional and perceptual processes can be dramatically biased by deep psychological mechanisms. The present study further explores the nature of perceptual biases in a patient with RHD and an anosodiaphoric reaction to cognitive impairment. The patient was asked to tell a story, depicting the events in three Thematic Apperception Test (TAT) cards. The patient's descriptions revealed systematic distortions of several “objective” features of characters and scenes, which enabled him to view the pictures as exact portrayals of episodes from his own life. These “pure projective” distortions are examined in light of three theories: Ramachandran's lateralization of “schema sorting” and “incongruency detection” functions; Kaplan-Solms and Solms's theory of narcissistic regression in right peri-sylvian lesions; and the Process Approach. Finally, I consider possible implications of these findings for normal, everyday instances, in which visual perception is massively colored by projective mechanisms.

Generalized Brain Arousal Mechanisms Contributing to Libido

Donald Pfaff , Eugene Martin and Lee-Ming Kow

Lee-Ming Kow

1230 York Avenue, New York, NY 10021, U.S.A. mailto:pfaff@rockefeller.edu

New York, NY, U.S.A.

Lee-Ming Kow  

arousal; estrogen; histamine; hypothalamus; libido; norepinephrine; opioid; preoptic area; prostaglandina

This theoretical paper proposes that underlying the concept of libido is a primitive set of brain mechanisms responsible for the generalized arousal of the central nervous system and the activation of all behavioral responses. Having given the concept of “generalized CNS arousal” an operational definition, we write an equation that describes how specific motivational needs are integrated with generalized arousal to produce an overall state of the CNS sufficient for potentiating behavioral responses. Factor analysis of behavioral data with mice suggests that among all CNS arousal-related influences, generalized arousal contributes about a third of the variance. Many neuroanatomical, neurophysiological, and genomic mechanisms for arousal are reviewed here. Highlighted are large reticular formation neurons in the medullary medulla whose axons bifurcating rostrally and caudally equip them to contribute, respectively, both to cerebral cortical arousal and to autonomic arousal. Their rapid responses would cause sudden changes in CNS state associated with, for example, states of panic. Consequences of the actions of generalized arousal networks include increased alertness and attention that serve all cognitive functions and all emotional expression. Specifically with respect to psychoanalytic concepts, these networks provide the psychic energy necessary for the expression of libido.

This year the Istanbul Neuro-Psychoanalysis Study Group focused on activities that will spread the neuropsychoanalytic approach among the specialists in Istanbul and interdisciplinary brainstorming and further research.

On 24 January 2007, the first panel of the Turkish Psychological Association Istanbul Branch was organized by our group. The panel “Neuro-Psychoanalysis in Istanbul!” was directed by Professor Giiler Fis, ek from the Psychology Department of Bogazici University. Speakers included clinical psychologist Fatma Gokce Ozkarar from Nisan Psychotherapy Center and psychiatrist Saffet Murat Tura from Imago Psychotherapy Center. Ozkarar presented an introductory overview of the neuropsychoanalytic approach to body-mind dualism, how Eastern philosophy of mind can provide wholeness for the approach, and how neuropsychoanalysis can be implemented in psychotherapeutic settings. On the other hand, Tura discussed the main epistemological problem of neuropsychoanalytic approaches and how quantum physics may be utilized to understand body-mind dualism. About 60 participants from different disciplines and affiliations attended the panel, and their questions and comments contributed to the integration of knowledge.

On 15 March 2007, §eyma Dogramaci, the director of Nisan Psychotherapy Center, invited Serkant Cetin, a doctor of physics at Dogus University, to give an introductory seminar to psychotherapists about quantum physics. Links between quantum physics and psychology, and the relationship between matter and energy, were discussed in further detail. This was an initial step to explore how we can make use of the main principles of quantum physics to understand body-mind dualism.

At the 8th Neuro-Psychoanalysis Congress held in Vienna in July 2007, Fatma Gokce Ozkarar presented her research entitled “The Utilization of the Emotional Stroop Test to Analyze Self-Object Representations in Depression.” Her research studied the role of frontal lobe hypoactivation in the mechanism of splitting observed in the self-object representations of depressed individuals. The study also aimed to demonstrate that the Emotional Stroop Test, as a neuro-psychological task, can be utilized as a tool to investigate the predictions of object relations theory.

Response to Commentaries

Douglas Watt

Douglas Watt

Douglas Watt  

Affirmative Action for Emotion in Cognitive Neuroscience?

First of all, let me just say that I am most grateful to all of the reviewers for such thoughtful and highly detailed commentaries, which often pointed out aspects to the literature and dimensions to what is clearly such a complex problem, aspects to which I had not given adequate thought (or, in many instances, had not had adequate time to think about or digest!). In general, although several commentaries were supportive of the general argument, some of the comments make it clear that I was not as successful as I might have hoped in attempting to outline a more integrated view of empathy as a process of necessity sitting on the emotion-cognition border. Two commentaries thought that I had given insufficient weight to mirror neuron systems (MNSs) in terms of their contribution to embodied simulation and to empathy, and in general the more “affectively oriented” the research and professional background of the commentator, the more accepting the commentator was of the basic argument in the target article. Of course, this does not suggest that I was as successful as I had hoped or, in any case, that my arguments were less than fully persuasive. I remain cautiously optimistic that in my response to commentaries, I can clarify some issues raised and suggest some future tests that might better bridge these domains of cognition and emotion.

Some preliminary general comments

Emotion cannot be reduced to just another form of cognitive processing, or “annexed” as some researchers and theorists have proposed (see Lane & Nadel, 2000). The border remains a mostly unmapped territory where we have few clearly established first principles by which to understand or structure the admittedly complex and reciprocal interactions between emotion and cognition, in which emotion has to be seen as directing and motivating cognitive processing, while cognition inhibits as well as activates and even blends various primary emotional currents. Empathy has to be considered a place where these critical reciprocal influences on the border of emotion and cognition could be mapped, but very few have offered even a stab at general principles. I hope that at least this effort underlines that empathy is in fact on the cognition-emotion border, even if we still are somewhat divided about the relative importance of the two sides or about how emotion and cognition come together. My primary motivation was to re-underline the critical roles of emotion and to stress empathy's close connections to social bonding and prosocial emotional states, as a necessary part of the “alloy” of emotion and cognition in this process.

Hemispheric Asymmetry and the Diversity of Emotional Experience in Anosognosia

Mona Tondowski , Zsofia Kovacs , Catherine Morin and Oliver Turnbull

Oliver Turnbull

(Bangor, U.K.)

(Paris)

(Bangor, U.K.)

Oliver Turnbull  

A long-standing question in neuropsychology has been whether basic emotions are lateralized in one hemisphere in the brain. A more recent, controversial, conceptualization has been that both hemispheres process emotion, but the left is specialized for positive emotions and the right for negative emotions. This claim has been partially bolstered by the claim that denial of deficit (anosognosia) results from a loss of negative emotions after right-sided lesions. A range of objections have been raised to this account. These include the analytically inspired suggestion that anosognosia might result from an emotion-regulation deficit, associated with changes in body image, producing ill-maintained defenses against aspects of reality that are difficult to tolerate. The present study involved presenting emotion-related stimuli to each hemispace of anosognosic patients and measuring emotional experience. Across three different assessment methods, the anosognosic patients were able to experience the full range of emotions, independent of location. In addition, the magnitude of the anosognosia was not obviously related to lesion size and location and may reflect differences in premorbid personality. These findings run counter to the claim of a hemispheric asymmetry in positive vs. negative emotion and are consistent with the psychoanalytically inspired claim that the right hemisphere plays a substantial role in emotion regulation, rather than in the experience of a single class of emotion.

emotions, lateralization, diversity, experience, anosognosia

A long-standing question in neuropsychology has been whether basic emotions are lateralized in one hemisphere in the brain (Heilman, Scholes, & Watson, 1975; Mills, 1912; Sackeim & Gur, 1978; Springer & Deutch, 1998), an issue that has long been important for the question of how psychoanalytic models might map onto the brain (e.g., Galin, 1974). One clear research trend is that the left hemisphere tends to be more specialized for a number of cognitive processes, whereas the right hemisphere seems to be more involved in processing all classes of emotion (Borod, 1992; Borod, Koff, Yecker, Santschi, & Schimdt, 1998; Mandal, Mohanty, Pandey, & Mohanty, 1996; Springer & Deutch, 1998). For example, many studies (e.g. Borod, 1992; Borod, Bloom, Brickman, Nakhutina, & Curko, 2002; Heilman, Scholes, & Watson, 1975; Kucharska-Pietura, Phillips, Gernand, & David, 2003; Mandal et al., 1996) have found that patients with right-hemisphere lesions showed problems in recognizing emotional facial expression (Borod, 1992; Kucharska-Pietura et al., 2003; Mandal et al., 1996) and in identifying perceptual or auditory cues to emotion (Borod, Bloom, Brickman, Nakhutina, & Curko, 2002; Ehran, Borod, Tenke, & Bruder, 1998; Kucharska-Pietura et al., 2003). Other studies (e.g., Mandal et al., 1996; Sackheim & Gur, 1978) have shown that stimuli presented to the left visual field (i.e. to the right hemisphere first) were judged as more emotional (Dimberg & Petterson, 2000; Ley & Bryden, 1979; Mandal et al., 1996; Nakamura et al., 1999) and that the left side of the face was considered to express emotion more intensely than the right side of the face (Borod, Haywood, & Koff, 1997; Borod et al., 1998; Carriba, Loeches, Morcillo, & Hopkins, 2002; Sackheim & Gur, 1978).

Jean Stora

JBSTORA@aol.com

Jean Stora  

In October 2006, with Professor J.-F. Allilaire, the head of the Department of Psychiatry and Professor M.-O. Bitker, Department of Urology, we launched a new diploma at the Faculty of Medicine: “Integrative Psychosomatics, Psychoanalysis, Medicine and Neurosciences.” It is a new approach developed in a recent publication by Jean Benjamin Stora: La neuro-psychanalyse (2006). This is the first publication in French presenting the neuropsychoanalytic approach developed by Mark Solms and others. In chapter 5 of the book the author proposes a neuropsychosomatic approach to the stages of psychosexual maturation, amplifying Freud's theory in relation to somatopsychic organizations. In conclusion, he indicates the need to develop a meta-model derived from both metapsychology and neuroscience to meet the challenges posed by the neurobiologi-cal view of thought. The author proposes that beside the classic neuropsychoanalytic approach, there is room for a neuropsy-chosomatic line dealing more with the neurohormonal system. Man is not only neuronal but basically psycho-neuro-hormonal. In June 2007 Karnac published a new book by Stora entitled When the Body Displaces the Mind, presenting a new approach to body-mind relations with a view to achieving better understanding and therefore better treatment of patients suffering from somatic diseases, with a preface written by Mark Solms. The author postulates the existence of somatopsychic organizations throughout the process of psychosexual development, thus supplementing in the somatic domain the developmental stages (oral, anal, phallic, and genital) proposed by Freud to make these into comprehensive organizations that are no longer restricted to the psychic apparatus. Thus the psyche is no longer separated from the body, and the body-mind dichotomy is removed, giving way to a continual process of integration of the psyche, the organic functions, and the central nervous system, which occurs during the first twenty years of life in human beings.

Bulletin 16: Introduction

We are happy to introduce a new member in our league: The Neuroscience and Psychoanalysis Discussion Group of the West Midlands Institute of Psychotherapy, England. Since the first issue of our Journal in 1999 and the founding of our Society in July 2000, I [I.M.] have been corresponding with about 30 groups and societies around the world, studying or working within the new field of neuropsychoanalysis and body/mind issues. Most of the groups are continuing their studies, in one way or another, some going into the hard work of empirical research. During these years, editing the reports received for the Bulletin has been a rather lonely and time-consuming job. Now I am no longer alone at this task. Maggie Zellner, in New York, has volunteered to give a helping hand and be my editorial assistant. Those of you who have attended our Congresses know her well from the Education Days, where she has done a tremendous job lecturing about the structure and function of the brain. This time she has done the heavy part of the editing. I am deeply thankful to her. This also means that if you have any questions related to our work in the society, and especially the Bulletin, you can write to Maggie Zellner (magsterz@gmail.com) as well as to me. Please do not hesitate to contact us.

Waves of the Unconscious: The Neurophysiology of Dreamlike Phenomena and Its Implications for the Psychodynamic Model of the Mind

Robin Carhart-Harris

Robin Carhart-Harris

Whitson St, Bristol, BS1 3NY (email: R.carhart-harris@bris.ac.uk).

Robin Carhart-Harris  

unconscious, psychoanalysis, dissociation, dream, déjà vu, lysergic acid diethylamide

This paper reviews scientific literature on four subjective states: the dream state, the dreamy state of temporal lobe epilepsy and temporal lobe stimulation, the acute psychotic state, and the psychedelic state. Evidence is cited showing that underlying the emergence of dreamlike phenomena in all four states is the occurrence of high-voltage bursts of theta and slow-wave activity (2-8 Hz) in the medial temporal lobes. The medial temporal regions are recognized to play an important role in memory and emotion. In the dream state, medial temporal lobe bursts are tightly correlated with PGO waves. It has been widely speculated that PGO waves are direct neurophysiological correlates of dreaming. On a phenomenological level, the dream state, the dreamy state, the acute psychotic state, and the psychedelic state have all been viewed as conducive to the emergence of unconscious material into consciousness. An argument is made that bursts of electrical activity spreading from the medial temporal lobes to the association cortices are the primary functional correlate of discharging psychical energies, experienced on a subjective level as the emergence of unconscious material into consciousness. The implications of these findings for the scientific legitimacy of the psychodynamic model are discussed.

Commentary on “Toward a Neuroscience of Empathy: Integrating Affective and Cognitive Perspectives”

Lucy Biven and Jaak Panksepp

Jaak Panksepp

Leicester, U.K.

Pullman WA, U.S.A.

Jaak Panksepp  

Emotion-Cognition Mind/Brain Interpenetration in Empathy

Douglas Watt is well aware of the difficulties inherent in the neuroscientific study of higher-order emotions, as he provides the most extensive integration, to date, for understanding brain substrates of empathy. He emphasizes that empathy, like all affective cognitions, lies at the intersection of consciousness and emotion. Just as there are different emotions and levels of individual emotional complexities (from primary to tertiary processes), there are different levels of empathic feelings and consciousness. Watt develops an argument hypothesizing that deep empathy is fundamentally an emotional function, based largely on a social-engagement and attachment cluster of emotions (LUST, PLAY, CARE/NURTURANCE, and PANIC/SEPARATION DISTRESS: here we will simply use the original designators CARE and PANIC for the nurturance and separation-distress systems respectively), secondarily honed by the defense cluster (FEAR, RAGE, and disgust), all elaborated by higher cognitive consider-ations.1

Watt explains that empathy interdigitates with attachment systems for the following reasons:

Empathy prevents us from hurting people we love, and this maintains the integrity of attachments.

Empathy helps to protect us from the anguish of broken attachments: since humans are profoundly social creatures, we are vulnerable to the ravages of loss. Perhaps empathy evolved as a buffer against the misery of loss, providing a means of comfort.

People and animals are more apt to display empathy toward others with whom they already have an emotional attachment.

Secure early attachments engender the child's capacity to empathize, whereas ambivalent attachments engender an unhappy self-absorption that interferes with the ability to empathize.

Watt emphasizes the importance of empathy in psychotherapy, highlighting how failures in parental empathy can result in faulty childhood attachments. Ideal therapeutic settings can recruit empathic resonances to help repair deficits in attachment.
